bullets: Diversification functions as the closest thing to a free lunch for individual investors — little is given up while removing the biggest way people ruin themselves: one position going to zero at the worst possible time.
Risk management for individuals is mostly behavioral rather than mathematical; sitting still while a holding gets cut in half is the hard part, and diversification makes that survivable.

Concentration with deep understanding beats diversification, according to the opposing view — spreading across a hundred names means owning things you can't judge, which amounts to ignorance, evenly distributed rather than safety.

A portfolio is a system of correlated bets; a handful of deeply understood positions is argued to be more robust because their co-movement is visible, whereas diversifying without understanding hides the correlation until it's the only thing that matters.

Account data on retail investors showed concentrated accounts had far fatter tails — cited as measured evidence that concentration is how retail investors blow themselves up and diversification is the only real risk control.

The decisive question is whether an investor's edge survives contact with their own behavior rather than diversify-or-not — concentration compounds a durable edge, while no amount of diversification saves one that doesn't hold up.
